description: We're a team of five university students ready to turn crazy ideas into reality! 🚀 We love science, technology, innovation, and solving real-world problems. We're looking for creative, ambitious teammates with skills in programming, AI, data analysis, engineering, design, or scientific research. Most importantly, we want curious minds, bold thinkers, and people who aren't afraid to experiment. Got skills, wild ideas, and a passion for innovation? Let's build something out of this world!
summary: Our project is an interactive website that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion archive into answers for the Moon and Mars habitats now being designed. It brings together 24 investigations from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics system and the Saffire IV–VI reports: 1,517 tests and 10,107 measured values, each traced to its source. For any mission atmosphere, it summarizes every investigation, ranks them by relevance with adjustable weights, and maps what NASA has never tested. Three machine-learning models trained on NASA flight data predict whether a cabin material keeps burning, how long a gas flame survives without ventilation, and how fast fuel droplets burn, each with an uncertainty range and a warning when conditions fall outside what NASA tested. Exact Shapley (SHAP) values explain each prediction input by input. A retrieval-augmented AI chat answers questions only from 4,086 passages of NASA reports and cites them. Physics simulations, audience-specific views and a downloadable crew briefing complete the tool.
details:
What it does and how it works

Flame in Freefall turns NASA's microgravity combustion archive into decisions for the habitats now being designed, where the air is expected to be about 30 % oxygen at 0.69 atm. We collected 24 investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system and the Saffire IV–VI reports. Python loaders turn them into one dataset with consistent units: 1,517 tests and 10,107 measured values, each traced to its source file and line. Every one of the 103 corrections and source conflicts is logged.

Users pick a mission atmosphere, and the site recomputes everything for it:

Summaries: for each investigation, its hardware, samples, instruments, what changed between tests, and its key result.

Ranking: a transparent relevance score with adjustable weights, a reason for every row, and the real tests closest to the mission air.

Predictions from three models trained on NASA flight data:

- whether a cabin material keeps burning (gradient boosting with physics constraints, ROC-AUC 0.958);

- how long a gas flame survives with the fans off (a survival model that correctly handles flames still burning at fuel cut-off);

- how fast fuel droplets burn (a Gaussian process, validated against 188 measured burn times).

Each prediction carries an uncertainty range and a warning when conditions fall outside what NASA tested.

Explanations: exact Shapley (SHAP) values show how much each input moved a prediction.

Ask the archive: a retrieval-augmented AI chat that answers only from 4,086 passages of NASA reports and cites them.

Gaps: what NASA has never tested near the mission air, with five recommended experiments.

Benefits

Engineers get design numbers and a downloadable crew briefing in minutes instead of reading dozens of reports.

Researchers see which data apply to their conditions, and where the data run out.

Students and professors get guided lessons and interactive physics.

Every number is labelled as a NASA measurement, model prediction, NASA literature, physics estimate or data gap, so nothing is presented as more certain than it is.

Intended impact

Safer fire-safety design for lunar and Martian habitats, and better-targeted NASA experiments. One headline result: in oxygen-rich air, shutting off ventilation may not put a fire out. Our model predicts flames burn about 4.6 times longer than in Earth cabin air. Another: smoke detection has never been tested at habitat conditions.

Tools and languages

Python: pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, lifelines, pytest.

Website: JavaScript with React, Vite and three.js; FastAPI serves the models live.

Dashboard: Streamlit with Plotly.

AI chat: LangChain, LangGraph and ChromaDB. Answers come from Google Gemini or Gemma 4 via OpenRouter.

Hosting: GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages; the site is also packaged in a Docker container.

No hardware.

AI disclosure: Claude (Anthropic) assisted development; all AI use is declared.

Creativity

Physics in the models: extra oxygen or pressure can never lower the predicted chance of burning.

Exact explanations: Shapley values are computed exactly, not sampled.

Moon and Mars: answers are bounded between our 0 g and 1 g data, plus buoyancy physics, and never presented as measurements.

Interactive 3D: an Earth, Moon and Mars scene and animated flame simulators.

Audience views: separate paths for undergraduates, graduate students, professors, researchers and engineers.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty: models are validated on tests they never saw, every number shows its evidence type, and missing data stay missing.

Traceability: every value links back to its source.

Data gaps: we report them openly rather than hide them.

Accessibility: keyboard use, reduced motion and mobile layouts.

Open licences: NASA data CC0, our code Apache-2.0.

Safety disclaimer: this is a research and education tool, not a certified fire-safety system.
